meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

выпить.gloss: to drink (up); to have a drink

meanings.en: to drink (up); to have a drink
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'пить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to drink (up); to have a drink', paired with 'пить'.

related.gloss: to go on a drinking binge

examples.trans: May I drink a tiny drop of beer?
Is there anything to drink?

examples.text: Милый, можно я выпью капельку пива?
examples.trans: Darling, may I drink a tiny drop of beer?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'мечательный'). Qualitative adjective formed with the productive suffix '-тельный'/'-ливый'. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('wonderful, remarkable').

examples.trans: Made wonderful crafts.
This is wonderful news.

examples.text: Все наши юные творцы сделали замечательные поделки!
examples.trans: All our young creators made wonderful crafts!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'person; (pl) people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is a good person.
There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm thinking about it.
We're talking about the town.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'много'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.
I'm a bit tired.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'жасно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Terrible! A very bad suit!
It is terribly cold outside today.

examples.text: Ужасно. Зачем вы мне это рассказываете?
examples.trans: Awful. Why are you telling me this?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тыдно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: It's shameful!
I'm ashamed.

examples.text: Подожди, Нин, ты не поняла. Это же стыдно!
examples.trans: Wait, Nina, you don't get it. It's shameful!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'left'.

examples.text: Вика, ну он одинокий. Я же не оставлю его одного.
examples.trans: Vika, come on, he's all alone. I can't just leave him on his own.

examples.text: Я же не оставлю его одного.
examples.trans: I can't just leave him on his own.

examples.text: Ты что, голову в Москве оставил?
examples.trans: What, did you leave your head in Moscow?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'dinner' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

examples.text: Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.
Vegetable stew for dinner?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('friendly').

examples.trans: That was simply friendly advice.

examples.text: Мне нужна одна небольшая дружеская услуга.
examples.trans: I need one small friendly favor.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'company, firm; group of friends' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: And that is Osipenko's cousin's company!
He works at a large company.

examples.text: Не все компании такие добрые, как наша.
examples.trans: Not all companies are as kind as ours.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Even I feel a bit ashamed right now.
It became somehow quiet in the room.
For long? You need to convince me somehow!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ъесть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to eat up', paired with 'есть'.

examples.text: Скоро. А пока я есть хочу, слона бы съел!
examples.trans: Soon. But for now I'm hungry, I could eat an elephant!

examples.text: А пока я есть хочу, слона бы съел!
examples.trans: But for now I'm hungry, I could eat an elephant!

examples.text: Лютик, где ты это находишь? Что он опять съел?
examples.trans: Lyutik, where do you find this stuff? What did he eat again?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine there.
Who's there?
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common masculine noun meaning 'fridge' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The milk is in the fridge.
Whose fridge is this?

examples.text: Курица? Нет. А чей это холодильник?
examples.trans: Chicken? No. And whose fridge is this?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'мидоры'). Common masculine noun meaning 'tomatoes' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Шеф, там картошку и помидоры привезли.
examples.trans: Chef, they delivered potatoes and tomatoes there.
Here are my new apartments.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'man, real man, bloke' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: You should have acted like a real man!
He's a decent bloke.

examples.text: Что мы, мы? Тебе надо было как мужик!
examples.trans: What do you mean, we? You should have acted like a man!

поехать.gloss: to go (by vehicle), to set off

meanings.en: to go (by vehicle), to set off
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go (by vehicle), to set off', paired with 'ехать'.

examples.trans: We'll go home.
All right, Arkashenka. We'll be off, it's time.
Right, I'm off!

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'karaoke' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Одно дело в караоке руку сломать.
examples.trans: Breaking an arm at karaoke is one thing.

examples.text: Одно дело в караоке руку сломать. А другое — обидеть человека на всю жизнь.
examples.trans: Breaking an arm at karaoke is one thing. And hurting a person for life is another.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'when', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: When I grow up, I'll be the mayor.
Oh yeah? When?

examples.text: Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
examples.trans: When I grow up, you'll be begging me to forgive you!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('necessary, needed').

examples.trans: I need a job too.
Do you need a pen?
He needs money.

ехать.gloss: to go (by vehicle), to drive, to ride

meanings.en: to go (by vehicle), to drive, to ride
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to go (by vehicle), to drive, to ride', paired with 'поехать'.

examples.trans: Vitalik, we're going to the Santa Fe.

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем?
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'shower' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Straight from the shower.

examples.text: Они выложили фотографию прямо из душа.
examples.trans: They posted a photo straight from the shower.

examples.text: Пока ты не сходишь в душ.
examples.trans: Before you go take a shower.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'romance, novel' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Никто не узнает про наш тайный роман.
examples.trans: No one will find out about our secret romance.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sleep', paired with 'поспать'.

examples.trans: Let's go to sleep.
The child is already asleep.

examples.text: Ладно, утром позвоню ей. Поехали спать.
examples.trans: All right, I'll call her in the morning. Let's go to sleep.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'stop!, cut!', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Stop, that's a wrap!
Stop, you cannot go any further!
Stop, that's a wrap! Good job, Samson!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: May I have a look?
Can you smoke here?
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'a minute' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Соседи, привет! Слушай, дружок, дай свой телефон на минутку.
examples.trans: Hi, neighbours! Listen, buddy, lend me your phone for a minute.

examples.text: Слушай, дружок, дай свой телефон на минутку.
examples.trans: Listen, buddy, lend me your phone for a minute.
Doctor, wait a minute, please!
